title: Johnson–Claisen rearrangement
subtitle: An allylic alcohol and triethyl orthoacetate give a γ,δ-unsaturated ester
conditionsLabel: MeC(OEt)₃ (excess), propanoic acid (cat.), 140 °C, ethanol distilled off

mixed-orthoester.caption: the mixed orthoester from but-2-en-1-ol and triethyl orthoacetate, with propanoic acid
mixed-orthoester.learnerPrompt: The alcohol has already swapped onto the orthoester (one ethanol lost). Now a second ethoxy group must go. Draw the first step.
hintTiers: Ethoxide is a poor leaving group. What does the acid catalyst do to make it a good one?
Propanoic acid protonates one of the two ethoxy oxygens, so ethanol can leave later. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from a lone pair on an ethoxy oxygen to the acidic hydrogen of propanoic acid. Arrow 2: from the O–H bond of the acid onto its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That oxygen can be protonated too, but then the butenol would leave and undo the exchange. Protonate an ethoxy oxygen: ethanol leaves and is distilled off, which drives the reaction on.
Ethoxide is a poor leaving group, and the solution is acidic. Protonate the oxygen first so that neutral ethanol leaves.

protonated-orthoester.caption: an ethoxy oxygen is protonated
protonated-orthoester.learnerPrompt: Now the protonated group can leave. Draw it going, helped by a neighbouring oxygen.
hintTiers: When ethanol leaves, the central carbon is left short of electrons. A lone pair next door can fill the gap.
The C–O bond to the protonated oxygen breaks and the other ethoxy oxygen pushes in a lone pair to make C=O⁺. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from the bond between the central carbon and the protonated oxygen onto that oxygen. Arrow 2: from a lone pair on the other ethoxy oxygen to its bond with the central carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That oxygen is not protonated, so it would leave as an alkoxide. The bond that breaks is the one to the protonated oxygen.

oxocarbenium-ion.caption: the dialkoxycarbenium ion, with ethanol and propanoate
oxocarbenium-ion.learnerPrompt: Propanoate is a weak base, but strong enough here. Make the ketene acetal.
hintTiers: The cation is stabilised by its two oxygens. Which hydrogens are now acidic, and what does losing one make?
Propanoate removes a hydrogen from the methyl group; its pair makes a C=C and the C=O⁺ pair moves back onto oxygen. Three arrows: a ketene acetal.

Arrow 1: from a lone pair on a propanoate oxygen to a methyl hydrogen. Arrow 2: from that C–H bond to the bond between the methyl carbon and the central carbon. Arrow 3: from the C=O⁺ π bond onto the ethoxy oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Propanoate can add to the cation, but that is reversible and leads nowhere. Losing a proton from the methyl group gives the ketene acetal that can rearrange.
That is the last step run backwards. Ethanol is distilled off at 140 °C, so it does not come back.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Two of three: the central carbon would have five bonds. Move the C=O⁺ π pair back onto oxygen.

ketene-acetal.caption: the ketene acetal, drawn curled so its ends meet
ketene-acetal.learnerPrompt: At 140 °C the ketene acetal rearranges. Draw the single step.
hintTiers: The ketene acetal is an allyl vinyl ether: C=C, oxygen, then the butenyl group. Count six atoms round a ring.
The O–CH₂ bond breaks, the CH₂ end of the ketene acetal bonds to the far alkene carbon (the one carrying the methyl group), and the oxygen gets a C=O. Three arrows.

Arrow 1: from the ketene acetal C=C π bond to a new bond between its CH₂ and the alkene carbon carrying the methyl group. Arrow 2: from the O–CH₂ σ bond to the bond between that oxygen and the central carbon (it becomes C=O). Arrow 3: from the butenyl C=C π bond to the bond between its other CH and the CH₂ that lost oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the O–CH₂ bond on its own would give an ester enolate and an allyl cation. In the Claisen rearrangement it breaks only as the new C–C bond forms, in one cyclic step.
The ethyl group is a bystander that ends up in the ester. The bond that breaks is the one to the butenyl CH₂.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the new C–C bond. Now the oxygen side: the O–CH₂ bond becomes a C=O π bond, and the butenyl π bond moves across. Two more arrows.

ester.caption: ethyl 3-methylpent-4-enoate, with ethanol and propanoic acid

steps.explanationAfterStep: A proton transfer turns an ethoxy group into a good leaving group, neutral ethanol. Either ethoxy group will do: they are the same.

Ethanol leaves, pushed out by a lone pair on a neighbouring oxygen: the same step as in acetal hydrolysis. The cation is shared over the carbon and both oxygens. At 140 °C the ethanol boils off, which pulls every exchange step forward.

Loss of a proton next to the cation gives a ketene acetal, a C=C carrying two oxygens. Propanoic acid is given back, so it is a catalyst. This ketene acetal is never isolated: it rearranges as soon as it forms.

A [3,3]-sigmatropic shift: a Claisen rearrangement. The new C–C bond goes to the far end of the allylic alcohol's alkene, so the alkene moves to the end of the chain (an allylic transposition), and the product is a γ,δ-unsaturated ester. Through a chair transition state a chiral secondary allylic alcohol passes its configuration to the new stereocentre, and an E-alkene is formed in the chain when there is one. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges and no E/Z marks.

mechanismSummary: In the Johnson orthoester Claisen rearrangement, an allylic alcohol is heated with excess triethyl orthoacetate and a trace of propanoic acid. The alcohol first exchanges onto the orthoester (protonation, ethanol leaves, the alcohol adds, a proton is lost: the same steps as acetal exchange, shown here only from the mixed orthoester onwards). A second ethanol is then lost to give a dialkoxycarbenium ion, which loses a proton to give a ketene acetal. This allyl vinyl ether undergoes a [3,3]-sigmatropic shift to a γ,δ-unsaturated ester, two carbons longer, with the alkene moved along. Distilling off ethanol drives every equilibrium forward. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges and no E/Z marks.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 35
W. S. Johnson, L. Werthemann, W. R. Bartlett, T. J. Brocksom, T.-T. Li, D. J. Faulkner and M. R. Petersen, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1970, 92, 741
